{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals that German legal texts contain person entities in two main contexts: judges/lawyers (often with titles like Dr., Mag., Univ.-Prof., Hofrat) and parties in the case (plaintiffs/defendants). The key challenge is distinguishing between titles that are part of the name versus titles that are part of a job description, and capturing full names which may include multiple words, suffixes (MBA, Bakk. iur.), or compound surnames.",
  "strategy": "Use specific regex patterns to capture names preceded by common German academic/professional titles and names appearing in legal party contexts, ensuring capture groups isolate the name text for accurate span extraction.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use capture groups to extract the name while ignoring surrounding context like 'Dr.' or 'Hofrat' where appropriate, or including them if they are part of the standard entity representation in the text.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "judges_with_titles",
      "description": "Captures judges and officials with academic/professional titles (Dr., Mag., Univ.-Prof., Hon.-Prof., etc.)",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Senatspr\u00e4sident(?:in|en)?|Vizepr\u00e4sident(?:in)?|Hofrat(?:in)?|Hofr\u00e4t(?:in|innen)?|fachkundiger Laienrichter(?:in)?|Richter(?:in)?|Schriftf\u00fchrer(?:in)?|Generalprokurator(?:in)?|Anwalt(?:in)?|Rechtsanwalt(?:in)?|Rechtsanw\u00e4lt(?:in|e)|Rechtsanw\u00e4lte(?:-Partnerschaft)?|Partnerschaft|OG|GmbH|KG|CEG)\\s+(?:Univ\\.-?Prof\\.|Hon\\.-?Prof\\.|Prof\\.|Dr\\.|Mag\\.|MMag\\.|M\\.\\.?Mag\\.|B\\.\\.?Bakk\\.|Dipl\\.-?Ing\\.|DI\\.|PhD\\.|M\\.\\.?M\\.\\.?B\\.\\.?A\\.)?\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+MBA)?(?:\\s+und\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)?)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Matches judges and legal professionals with titles. The capture group $1 isolates the name part, handling various title formats and suffixes like MBA."
    },
    {
      "name": "parties_names",
      "description": "Captures names of parties (plaintiffs/defendants) in legal cases, often appearing after 'Partei' or 'gegen'",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:der\\s+(?:klagenden|beklagten|Antragsgegner|Antragsteller|Antragsgegnerin|Antragstellerin|betreibenden|verpflichteten)\\s+Partei|gegen\\s+die\\s+(?:beklagte|Antragsgegner)|gegen\\s+den\\s+(?:Beklagten|Antragsgegner)|der\\s+(?:klagenden|beklagten)\\s+Partei)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+MBA)?(?:\\s+und\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)?)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Captures party names in legal proceedings. The pattern looks for context markers like 'Partei' or 'gegen' to identify the person entity."
    },
    {
      "name": "criminal_defendants",
      "description": "Captures names of criminal defendants appearing after 'gegen' in criminal cases",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Strafsache gegen|Verbrechen der|Vergehen der)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
       
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "Specifically targets criminal defendants mentioned after 'Strafsache gegen' or crime descriptions."
    },
    {
      "name": "simple_names_with_context",
      "description": "Captures simple names that appear in specific legal contexts without titles",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:geboren am|im ersten Rechtsgang wurde|wurde schuldig erkannt|wurde freigesprochen)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 5,
      "reasoning": "Captures names in specific legal contexts like birth dates or verdict announcements where titles might be omitted."
    },
    {
      "name": "names_with_suffixes",
      "description": "Captures names that include academic or professional suffixes like Bakk. iur., Dipl.-Ing., etc.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Bakk\\. iur\\. |Dipl\\. -?Ing\\. |DI |PhD |MBA |M\\.\\.?M\\.\\.?B\\.\\.?A\\. )([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 4,
      "reasoning": "Handles names with specific academic/professional suffixes that appear before the name."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

Each rule needs:
- pattern: The regex pattern to match
- output_template: JSON template for each match, using variables:
  - $0: Full match text
  - $start: Start character offset
  - $end: End character offset
  - $1, $2, ...: Capture groups (regex only)
- output_key: Which output array to populate (e.g., "entities")

$0 vs $1: Use $0 when the full match IS the value. Use a capture group ($1) when you
need surrounding context for disambiguation — $start/$end auto-adjust to the group.
  Example: "prefix(\w+)" with "text": "$1" extracts only the captured part.
